title: No transfusion
stem:
You are an F2 doctor on a general medical ward. Mrs Grant, 70, has iron-deficiency anaemia with a haemoglobin of 68 g/L. She is breathless on exertion but otherwise stable. The team recommends a blood transfusion.

She refuses, saying she "doesn't want someone else's blood", and wants to go home. She has capacity.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Transfuse her in her best interests.
options.brief: Unlawful for a patient with capacity.
options.detailed: Best interests apply only to people who lack capacity.

options.text: Ask her about her reasons and concerns.
options.detailed: She may have worries about infection or other concerns that can be addressed. Exploring this respects her and supports an informed decision.

options.text: Insist she stays in hospital until her haemoglobin improves.
options.detailed: She has capacity and can decide to go home.

options.text: Explain the risks of declining, and alternatives such as IV iron.
options.brief: An informed decision needs the full picture.
options.detailed: There are alternatives, such as intravenous iron, which may be acceptable to her. Explaining the risks and options helps her decide.

options.text: Ask her family to persuade her to have the transfusion.
options.brief: Pressures her and involves them without consent.

options.text: Discharge her without follow-up, as she declined treatment.
options.brief: Respecting a refusal doesn't mean withdrawing care.
options.detailed: She still needs treatment for her anaemia and follow-up.

options.text: Refer her to psychiatry, as refusing blood is unusual.
options.brief: An unusual decision isn't evidence of lacking capacity.
options.detailed: She has capacity, and refusing blood isn't a psychiatric issue.

options.text: Respect her decision, and arrange a safe discharge plan.
options.brief: A capacitous refusal must be respected, with a safe plan.
options.detailed: She has capacity, so her decision must be respected. A clear plan for treatment, follow-up and safety-netting reduces the risk.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you respect a capacitous patient's refusal while making sure she is informed and safe.
explanation.keyDetails: She has capacity. She is stable. Alternatives exist.
explanation.reasoning: [B] explores her concerns, [D] informs her decision, and [H] respects it safely. The distractors override her ([A], [C]), pressure her ([E]), abandon her ([F]), or question her capacity without reason ([G]).
explanation.competing: [F] is the tempting option because it seems to respect her decision, but she still needs care.

references.title: Decision making and consent
references.note: Respecting the decisions of patients with capacity.
